projects.title: Sybil-Resilient Model Extraction Detection
projects.label: master's capstone · ML security
projects.one_line: Catching model-stealing attacks that hide across many fake (Sybil) accounts.
projects.headline_text: Sybil accounts caught: PRADA alone vs with my detection layer
projects.ask_keywords: capstone, sybil, model extraction, model stealing, prada, ml security
projects.intro: An extension of PRADA (Juuti et al., EuroS&P 2019), tested on an MNIST classifier. My master's capstone at Rutgers.
projects.question: PRADA spots model-stealing by checking whether an account's query distances look normally distributed. An attacker can split queries across fake (Sybil) accounts so each one stays under PRADA's 100-query warm-up and never gets checked.
projects.what_i_did: A second detection layer that compares query-distance histograms across accounts using Jensen-Shannon divergence. Sybil accounts all send Jacobian-generated images, so their histograms converge. Benign accounts' histograms don't.
projects.result: PRADA alone flagged **0 of 64** Sybil accounts. With the JS layer, detection held from 4 to 128 accounts with zero false positives.

key_numbers.label: Sybil accounts caught by PRADA alone
label agreement between the attacker's copy and the victim model

projects.recommendation: Run a cross-account check like this alongside per-account detection on any public model API, and re-tune the threshold on held-out traffic before relying on it in production.

images.alt: Detection rate vs number of Sybil accounts
images.caption: Detection rate as the attack is split across more fake accounts. PRADA alone drops to 0% at 64 accounts. The JS layer keeps firing, but from about 192 accounts up its separation signal weakens (see limitations below).

images.alt: PRADA W scores, attackers vs benign
images.caption: PRADA's single-account baseline. Attacker accounts score below the 0.96 threshold and get flagged. The benign account (0.9864) stays clean.

extra_sections.heading: How the test bed works
extra_sections.html: A CNN victim model (99.08% MNIST test accuracy) is served through a FastAPI endpoint that logs every query. A Papernot Jacobian-based attack runs 6 augmentation rounds to train a substitute model. PRADA (distance computation plus a Shapiro-Wilk test) and the JS layer are evaluated side by side, including a benign-user baseline and three query distributions: round-robin, randomized, and mixed 70/30.

extra_sections.heading: What it can't do
extra_sections.html:
• At 192 or more Sybil accounts, per-account histograms get sparse and the JS separation gap collapses, so detection becomes unstable.
  • A mixed 70/30 attack shrinks the separation gap to 0.002 in some configurations. Still detected, but the margin is thin.
  • The JS threshold (0.15) was tuned on the same data used for evaluation. There is no held-out test set.
  • PRADA's AUC of 1.0 comes from only two W scores, so I don't treat it as a robust result.

projects.title: F1 Pit Stop Strategy
projects.label: SQL + DAX
projects.one_line: Do faster pit stops actually win races?
projects.headline_text: correlation between total pit lane time and finishing position: more time, slightly worse finish (weak)
projects.ask_keywords: f1, formula 1, formula one, pit stop, racing, motorsport, constructor
projects.intro: 10,884 Formula 1 pit stops from 2011 to 2024, across six PostgreSQL tables.
projects.question: Does pit stop speed relate to where a driver finishes, and have stops gotten faster over the years?
projects.what_i_did: Tested the link at three levels (single stop, race average, race total) with CORR(), compared constructors with AVG and STDDEV, and tracked year-over-year change with LAG. In Power BI I rebuilt the Pearson correlation by hand in DAX and matched SQL's 0.175.
projects.result: The link is weak: **+0.135 to +0.175**. P1 finishers averaged 43.2s of pit lane time per race vs 57.0s for P18, but top teams tend to have both faster cars and faster crews, so pit speed alone doesn't explain results.

key_numbers.label: strongest correlation, total pit lane time vs finish
pit lane time got 1.29s slower from 2013 to 2014, the biggest year-over-year change
Red Bull average pit lane time (entry to exit), fastest and most consistent

projects.recommendation: Don't treat pit-crew speed alone as a lever for race results. Some teams' problem is consistency rather than speed: Aston Martin is mid-pack on speed but second-worst on variability, so that's where they have the most to gain.

images.alt: F1 pit stop strategy dashboard in Power BI
images.caption: My Power BI dashboard: pit lane time by finishing position and by season, plus speed vs consistency by constructor.

extra_sections.heading: Data cleaning
extra_sections.html: Stops of 100 seconds or longer were filtered out as red-flag and safety-car artifacts, so they wouldn't distort the averages.

projects.title: EvoStruct-Sub Protein Localization
projects.label: machine learning · bioinformatics
projects.one_line: Predicting where a protein ends up in or around a bacterial cell, from its sequence.
projects.headline_text: best 10-fold cross-validated accuracy (SVM), across three models
projects.ask_keywords: evostruct, protein, bioinformatics, biology, localization, bacteria
projects.intro: Applies the published EvoStruct-Sub method to a benchmark of 523 Gram-positive bacterial proteins in four subcellular locations. A Rutgers course project.
projects.question: Given only a protein's amino-acid sequence, can a model predict which of four locations it belongs to: cell membrane, cell wall, cytoplasm or extracellular?
projects.what_i_did: Combined evolutionary features from PSI-BLAST (PSSM) with structural features from SPIDER 2.0 into a 235-feature matrix, then trained and compared KNN, SVM and Random Forest with 10-fold cross-validation.
projects.result: Cross-validated accuracy: SVM **70.6%**, Random Forest 69.9%, KNN 66.0%. Accuracy on the training data was much higher (Random Forest 99.23%), which shows overfitting, so I report the cross-validated numbers.
projects.recommendation: Judge models on cross-validated accuracy, not training accuracy. To move past about 70%, tackle the class imbalance first (only 18 cell wall proteins) and reduce overfitting before adding more models.

extra_sections.heading: Reproducibility
extra_sections.html: Pre-extracted features and trained models are in the repo, so the classifiers run in about 10 minutes without the external tools. Rebuilding features from raw sequences needs PSI-BLAST and SPIDER 2.0 and takes several hours.

projects.ask_keywords: metaheuristic, optimizer, optimization algorithm, genetic algorithm, particle swarm, pso, wolf pack, grasshopper
projects.intro: Breast cancer classification on the UCI dataset.
projects.question: Instead of gradient descent, how well do metaheuristic optimizers train a classifier, and which one generalizes best?
projects.what_i_did: Implemented and compared the Grasshopper Optimization Algorithm, Wolf Pack Optimization, Particle Swarm Optimization and a Genetic Algorithm, tracking train and test accuracy and loss for each.
projects.result: In a single run, Wolf Pack and PSO tied at **97.37%** test accuracy, the Genetic Algorithm reached 96.49%, and Grasshopper lagged at 71.05%.
projects.recommendation: Use Wolf Pack or PSO for this kind of problem. Grasshopper needs parameter tuning before it is competitive.

ask.question: How do you gather requirements from stakeholders?
ask.keywords: gather requirements, gathering requirements, requirements gathering, requirement gathering, requirements, requirement, elicitation, stakeholder needs, discovery, understand the business, intake
ask.answer:
I start with the decision the stakeholder is trying to make, not the dashboard they think they want. I ask what problem they're solving, who will use the output, which KPIs matter and how often they need it.

Then I pin down definitions, because "active customer" or "SLA compliance" can mean different things to different teams. I document it as BRDs, FRDs, user stories and acceptance criteria, check the source data actually exists at the right level of detail, and review it with business and technical people before development starts. That saves a lot of rework in UAT.

ask.question: What's the difference between a BRD and an FRD?
ask.keywords: brd, frd, business requirements document, functional requirements document, difference between brd and frd, brd vs frd, requirements document, documentation
ask.answer:
The BRD says what the business needs and why. The FRD goes into how the solution should behave.

For example, the BRD might say marketing needs to see customer retention by segment. The FRD defines the metrics, filters, dimensions and business rules behind that.

At Adobe I write both, then break them into user stories and acceptance criteria, so there's a clear trail from the business problem through development and UAT.

ask.question: How do you define a KPI?
ask.keywords: kpi, kpis, define kpi, defining kpis, kpi definition, key performance indicator, metric, metrics, define a metric, measure success, success metrics, north star
ask.answer:
I start with the business goal behind it, because a metric without context misleads people. Then I write down the formula, numerator, denominator, grain, filters, time period, exclusions and source system, plus edge cases like cancelled orders or inactive customers.

Once it's agreed, I turn it into SQL and test it on sample records. At Adobe I define KPI and data-quality rules across Snowflake and Databricks and reconcile **25 KPIs** before executive reporting. The goal is that a KPI means the same thing to every team that looks at it.

ask.question: Tell me about your Power BI experience
ask.keywords: power bi, powerbi, pbi, dax, power query, power bi experience, measures, semantic model
ask.answer:
Power BI is my main reporting tool at Adobe. I built and own **8 Power BI dashboards** used by **20+ stakeholders** across marketing, product and customer experience, and they replaced manually assembled weekly decks.

I start from the KPI definitions, make sure the dataset has the right grain and reconciles with the source, and then design it so people can go from a top-line KPI down to trends and segments. When dashboards got slow, I pushed heavy aggregations down into the Snowflake/dbt layer.

In projects: a four-visual Olist dashboard on SQL views, and an F1 report where I rebuilt the Pearson correlation by hand in DAX and matched SQL's 0.175.

ask.question: What's your experience with Tableau?
ask.keywords: tableau, tableau experience, tableau dashboards, tableau prep
ask.answer:
Tableau was my main tool at Amazon. I delivered **10 Tableau dashboards** used by **30+ stakeholders** to track seller health, fulfillment performance, inventory and SLA compliance.

The data came from large Redshift tables, so I validated every dashboard against SQL output before release. I kept them focused: an operations manager needed to see quickly which seller or fulfillment area needed attention, not twenty charts.

ask.question: Power BI or Tableau: which do you prefer?
ask.keywords: prefer, preference, power bi vs tableau, tableau vs power bi, power bi or tableau, tableau or power bi, which tool, favorite tool, favourite tool, which is better, compare tools
ask.answer:
I've used both, so I don't have a strong favorite. My recent work at Adobe is Power BI, and I used Tableau heavily at Amazon.

I'd pick based on the company's ecosystem, data sources and users. The process is the same either way: define the KPI, prepare reliable data, validate it, then visualize it.

ask.question: How do you design a good dashboard?
ask.keywords: design a dashboard, dashboard design, good dashboard, build a dashboard, designing dashboards, dashboard best practices, best practices, usability, slow dashboard, dashboard performance, layout
ask.answer:
I start with the business question and the KPI definitions, not the visuals. Then I make sure the data underneath has the right grain and reconciles with the source.

The layout goes from the top-line KPI to trends to the detail, with filters and drill-downs so people don't need to ask me for a separate report. I keep it actionable rather than packed with charts, and I watch performance, because a fast, simple dashboard beats an impressive slow one. At Adobe I moved complex aggregations into the Snowflake/dbt layer to keep refreshes fast.

ask.question: Explain an ETL pipeline you worked on
ask.keywords: etl, elt, pipeline, pipelines, data pipeline, data pipelines, extract transform load, ingestion, data integration, source datasets, data flow
ask.answer:
At Amazon I built SQL-based ETL across **15 source datasets** of seller, order, inventory and fulfillment data, which fed daily operational reporting.

In the transform step I applied the business rules and shaped the data to the grain the KPIs needed. Validation was built in: duplicates, missing values, counts and KPI consistency. The output fed the recurring reports and the Tableau dashboards.

In my NFL project I also built a reproducible Python pipeline joining 25 seasons of game stats with weather data from two APIs.

ask.question: What's your experience with Snowflake and dbt?
ask.keywords: snowflake, dbt, data build tool, dbt models, dbt modeled, snowflake experience, data warehouse, warehouse, warehousing

My SQL over those models produces the segmentation logic behind **12 recurring stakeholder reports**, and I reconcile KPIs against Snowflake as part of source-to-report checks. I like that setup because the logic is defined once upstream, so different dashboards don't end up with different versions of the same metric.

ask.question: How do you do customer segmentation?

ask.question: Tell me about your cohort analysis experience

ask.question: What's your experience with forecasting?

ask.question: How have you used anomaly detection?
ask.keywords: anomaly, anomalies, anomaly detection, outlier, outliers, spike, spikes, unusual, unexpected change, alerts
ask.answer:
At Adobe I use anomaly detection to flag KPI outliers before the weekly stakeholder review, based on historical KPI patterns and statistical thresholds.

When something is flagged I don't assume it's real. I check the underlying data, recent pipeline changes and the KPI's history. If the data is right, it's a business trend worth explaining. If it's a data issue, it gets fixed before it reaches anyone.

ask.question: Tell me about a time you caught a discrepancy before executive reporting
ask.keywords: discrepancy, discrepancies, mismatch, mismatched, numbers didnt match, numbers dont match, wrong numbers, caught an error, caught a mistake, found an error, mistake, error in report
ask.answer:
At Adobe I reconcile **25 KPIs** from source to report before executive reporting. When one doesn't match, I first figure out whether the problem is in the source, the transformation or the report calculation.

I compare record counts and totals at each stage instead of debugging from the dashboard, narrow it to the KPI, time period or segment, and trace it back through the data flow. If it's a transformation issue I work with the technical team on the fix and validate the corrected output. It only goes to executives once it reconciles.

ask.question: Tell me about a data quality issue you handled
ask.keywords: data quality issue, data issue, bad data, dirty data, messy data, duplicate, duplicates, missing values, missing data, nulls, inconsistent data, clean data, data cleaning, cleaning
ask.answer:
At Amazon, inconsistent seller data sometimes threw off downstream KPIs. Profiling would surface duplicates, missing values or gaps between operational data and the calculated metrics.

Instead of patching the dashboard, I isolated which of the 15 source datasets caused the mismatch, compared source counts and totals with the reporting data, and traced the affected seller records. Once the source or transformation issue was fixed, I reconciled the KPI again before it went into executive reporting. Since then I treat validation as part of the analysis, not an afterthought.

ask.question: What do you do when a dashboard number looks wrong?
ask.keywords: root cause, root cause analysis, rca, number looks wrong, dashboard wrong, wrong number, debug, debugging, troubleshoot, troubleshooting, investigate, investigation, why did it drop, why did it change
ask.answer:
I work backward from the dashboard. First I confirm the KPI definition, filters, date range and grain, so I know what the right answer should be.

Then I run the SQL independently and compare it with the dashboard. If they still differ, I trace the metric through the transformation logic to the source, using counts and small samples to find exactly where the values split. After the fix I rerun the same reconciliation, and I check related KPIs, because one transformation bug often affects several.

ask.question: How would you optimize a slow SQL query?
ask.keywords: optimize, optimise, optimization, optimisation, slow query, slow queries, query performance, performance tuning, tuning, speed up, faster query, expensive query, execution plan
ask.answer:
First I work out where the cost comes from: data volume, joins, filters, aggregation or the data model.

Then I filter as early as possible, select only the columns I need, and check joins carefully, since a many-to-many join multiplies rows and hurts both speed and accuracy. Repeated heavy logic can move into a reusable reporting layer.

Afterward I compare both the runtime and the output totals with the original. A faster query is no use if it changes the answer.

ask.question: How do you approach exploratory data analysis?
ask.keywords: eda, exploratory, exploratory data analysis, explore data, exploring data, exploration, new dataset, first look, understand the data, distributions, patterns
ask.answer:
I look at structure and quality first: counts, nulls, duplicates, ranges and distinct values. Then distributions, relationships and anything odd.

In my Olist project I explored 99,441 orders across 27 states and 70+ categories before answering the business question, and that's how the link between late delivery and review score (-0.327 correlation) came up.

ask.question: How do you use statistics?
ask.keywords: statistics, statistical, statistical analysis, stats, correlation, regression, hypothesis, significance, sample size, trend analysis
ask.answer:
Mostly in practical ways. In Olist I used CORR() to measure late delivery against review score (-0.327). In F1 I rebuilt a Pearson correlation in DAX and matched SQL's 0.175. In the NFL project I compared win rates across temperature bands while watching sample sizes.

At work: statistical thresholds for KPI anomaly detection at Adobe, and trend and seasonality for fulfillment forecasting at Amazon.

ask.question: How do you handle conflicting stakeholder requirements?
ask.keywords: conflict, conflicts, conflicting, disagree, disagreement, disagreements, push back, pushback, difficult stakeholder, difficult stakeholders, competing priorities, competing requirements, priorities, prioritize, prioritise
ask.answer:
First I check whether people disagree on the goal or just on how to measure it. Usually it's two definitions of the same KPI or different levels of detail.

I write down both views and use real examples to show where the numbers differ, then bring it back to the business objective, the source of truth and the audience. If one definition can't serve both, I suggest a standard KPI or two clearly named metrics. Whatever is decided goes into the requirements and acceptance criteria, so it doesn't come back in UAT. My job isn't to pick a winner. It's to make the choice clear.

ask.keywords: challenging, challenge, challenges, hardest, difficult project, toughest, complex project, biggest challenge, most complex, proudest work

My Amazon supply chain work, because of the scale, the data quality and the impact. It meant 50M+ records across order, inventory, fulfillment and seller data, and the numbers had to be reliable enough for weekly operations decisions.

I built SQL ETL across 15 datasets with profiling and reconciliation, used cohort analysis to catch high-risk sellers, forecast peak-season volume, delivered the Tableau dashboards and automated the weekly reporting. ask.question: What's your biggest weakness?
ask.keywords: weakness, weaknesses, biggest weakness, greatest weakness, area of improvement, areas of improvement, improve on, working on, shortcoming, shortcomings, flaw, flaws
ask.answer:
I tend to trust people too quickly. If a teammate or another team hands me something, I assume they've already worked out the details, so I don't always dig into them myself.

In data work that's risky, because a number someone else prepared can still be wrong. So now I check the details myself before I rely on them: I profile the data, reconcile totals back to the source, and confirm the KPI definition instead of assuming it. That's a big part of why I reconcile 25 KPIs at Adobe before anything reaches executives.

ask.question: Tell me about a failure or mistake
ask.keywords: failure, failures, failed, fail, mistake, mistakes, setback, went wrong, lesson learned, lessons learned, learned from, what would you do differently
ask.answer:
At Amazon, the seller reporting I supported only showed a problem after a seller had already missed its SLA. Operations could react, but by then the breach had happened, so the reports weren't really helping anyone prevent it.

I changed the approach: I grouped sellers into cohorts and compared their fulfillment and SLA trends over time, so we could see which accounts were slipping before they breached. Operations used those lists for targeted intervention.

The lesson for me was that accurate reporting isn't enough. It has to show up early enough for someone to act on it.

ask.question: How do you handle tight deadlines and pressure?
ask.keywords: deadline, deadlines, tight deadline, tight deadlines, pressure, under pressure, stress, stressful, time pressure, urgent, urgent request, last minute, multiple deadlines, time management, manage your time
ask.answer:
Most of my work runs on a fixed rhythm, like weekly operations reviews at Amazon and weekly business reviews at Adobe, so I plan backward from the review and do the checks first, not last.

The biggest thing that helped was automating the repetitive part. At Amazon I cut weekly report prep from **6 hours to under 2**, and at Adobe a recurring report went from **9 hours to 5**. That leaves time for the analysis and validation instead of rushing them.

At Adobe, anomaly detection flags KPI outliers before the weekly review, so surprises get handled early, and in Jira I fix reporting defects within the sprint. When things really pile up, I agree on priorities with the stakeholder rather than quietly cutting the validation.
